note_claims.claim: The presenting complaint is a review of low mood occurring four weeks after starting sertraline.
The patient has experienced low mood for approximately three months.
The patient reports slight improvement in mood only in the mornings.
The patient reports reduced appetite and approximately half a stone weight loss.
The patient is currently signed off work as a warehouse supervisor for two weeks.
The patient reports passive suicidal ideation (wishing to not wake up) most days for the last two weeks.
The patient has no history of active suicidal thoughts, plans, or preparations.
The patient has no history of previous self-harm or suicide attempts.
Protective factors include the nephew and the mother.
The patient reports alcohol consumption of four cans most nights and sometimes more at the weekend.
The patient reports no drug use.
The patient experienced mild nausea in the first week of sertraline, which has since resolved.
The patient appears tired, has reduced eye contact, and has slowed speech, but speech is coherent.
The patient has no sign of psychotic features.
The patient's PHQ-9 score is 19.
The clinical impression is moderately severe depression with partial response to sertraline.
The patient presents with passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent, and protective factors are present.
The patient has harmful alcohol use.
The plan is to increase sertraline to 100 mg once daily.
The patient will be referred to the talking therapies service, and self-referral details will be provided.
The community mental health crisis team will be informed.
The follow-up appointment is scheduled in one week.
The patient agreed to hand stockpiled medicines to the sister.
The patient will be given details for an alcohol support service to help reduce consumption gradually.
A crisis plan was agreed: call NHS 111 (mental health option) or Samaritans 116 123 if thoughts worsen or acting on them; call 999 or go to A&E if unable to keep oneself safe.

transcript_facts.fact: The clinician greeted the patient and asked who was with them.
The patient's sister is named Laura.
The clinician asked if it was okay for Laura to stay for the whole appointment.
The patient wants his sister to stay for the appointment.
The patient started sertraline about four weeks ago.
The patient's mood has been 'not great,' with slight improvement in the mornings, but mostly the same.
The patient has been feeling low since the summer, which is about three months.
The patient's mood is rated as three, maybe two on a scale of nought to ten.
The patient reports bad sleep, waking up at four and lying there.
The patient reports reduced appetite and has lost about half a stone.
The patient is a warehouse supervisor and is signed off for another two weeks.
The patient reports passive suicidal ideation ('it'd be easier if I just didn't wake up') most days for the last couple of weeks.
The patient reports no active suicidal thoughts or plans.
The patient has no plans or preparations, such as getting hold of tablets.
The patient identifies his nephew and his mother as protective factors.
The patient reports no history of self-harm or suicide attempts.
The patient initially stated he was drinking four pints a week.
The relative corrected the frequency, stating he drinks four cans a night.
The patient confirmed the frequency, stating he drinks four cans most nights and sometimes more at the weekend.
The patient reports no drug use (cannabis or anything else).
The patient reported mild nausea in the first week of sertraline, which has now gone away.
The patient is taking sertraline every morning at a dose of fifty milligrams.
The clinician observed the patient looks tired, has reduced eye contact, and slowed speech, but is talking clearly and making sense.
The clinician noted there was no sign of anything like hearing voices.
The patient's PHQ-9 score is 19.
The clinician assessed the depression as moderately severe, noting only a small improvement after four weeks.
The clinician recommended increasing the sertraline dose to 100 milligrams once a day.
The clinician planned to refer the patient to the talking therapies service and provide self-referral details.
The clinician planned to inform the community mental health crisis team.
The clinician planned to review the patient in one week, rather than four.
The safety plan includes calling NHS 111 (mental health option) or Samaritans 116 123 if thoughts worsen or acting on them.
The safety plan includes calling 999 or going to A&E if the patient feels unable to keep himself safe.
The clinician asked if the patient would be willing to keep any stockpiled medicines out of the house or have the sister look after them.
The clinician planned to give details for a local alcohol support service to help reduce alcohol consumption gradually.
